                                   1

                                   2

                                   3

                                   4                                  UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                 NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6

                                   7     SANTIAGO TALAVERA CASTRO,                           Case No. 24-cv-06274-NW
                                                        Plaintiff,
                                   8
                                                                                             ORDER IMPOSING SANCTION AND
                                                  v.                                         DISCHARGING ORDER TO SHOW
                                   9
                                                                                             CAUSE
                                  10     FCA US, LLC,
                                                                                             Re: ECF Nos. 66, 95
                                                        Defendant.
                                  11

                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          The Court assumes familiarity with the background of this Song-Beverly Consumer

                                  14   Warranty Act (also known as lemon law) case, as outlined in the Court’s prior orders and the

                                  15   parties’ filings. See ECF Nos. 28, 31, 32, 43, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51, 57, 61, 66, 67, 95, 109, 111, 113.

                                  16          On July 14, 2026, the Court held an Order to Show Cause hearing with Plaintiff’s counsel,

                                  17   Payam Shahian and Larry Chae, and Defendant’s counsel, Michael Mehall, present. The Court

                                  18   reviewed on the record the history of the case, the series of events instigating the Court’s initial

                                  19   and follow up Orders to Show Cause, and counsels’ responses to those Orders.

                                  20          The Court focused on addressing the concern that animated its initial inquiry into

                                  21   Plaintiff’s counsel’s firm, Strategic Legal Practices (“SLP”), following SLP’s failure to file

                                  22   anything substantive in this case between July 31, 2024, when SLP initiated the action on behalf

                                  23   of Plaintiff Talavera Castro, and March 23, 2026; this includes SLP’s failure to file any of the

                                  24   myriad pretrial materials that were due on March 18, 2026, for a jury trial that was set to begin on

                                  25   April 13, 2026. For the Court to properly evaluate what sanction, if any, would be appropriate, the

                                  26   Court needed to understand whether there was an emergency, a reasonable mistake, or whether

                                  27   there was more serious or systemic misconduct that caused SLP’s failure to comply with Court

                                  28   Orders. The Court had a heightened concern because it learned that SLP counsel—the same
                                            Case 5:24-cv-06274-NW          Document 119        Filed 07/17/26    Page 2 of 5




                                   1   counsel of record in Mr. Talavera Castro’s case—had been sanctioned in another case in this

                                   2   District for lack of trial preparedness less than two weeks earlier. 1 See Lopez v. Ford Motor Co.,

                                   3   No. 24-CV-02155-BLF, 2026 WL 782497 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 19, 2026).

                                   4             The Court’s inquiry was further intended to elucidate whether SLP’s failure to comply

                                   5   with Court Orders was isolated to particular attorneys or was prevalent firm-wide. The Court soon

                                   6   learned that just the SLP lawyers who were counsel of record in this case had personally been

                                   7   sanctioned, in some instances in conjunction with a sanction to SLP, 31 times in less than 18

                                   8   months.

                                   9             During the Court’s April 22, 2026 continued hearing on the OSC, Ms. Carvalho (the SLP

                                  10   partner then assigned to this case) estimated that SLP currently had approximately 10,000 cases

                                  11   and only two partners, herself and Mr. Payam Shahian (the founder and managing partner). Ms.

                                  12   Carvalho then provided the Court with a hard copy of a March 26, 2026 order from the Central
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   District of California, a case in which Ms. Carvalho was also counsel of record. The judge

                                  14   imposed a $10,000 sanction against SLP but queried in the text of the order whether even that

                                  15   serious sanction was adequate. Brittany Michelle Chapman v. FCA US, LCC, No. 2:25- CV-

                                  16   07336-SB-SK, ECF No. 83, (C.D. Cal. Mar. 26, 2026). The first paragraph of that order states:

                                  17                    Plaintiff Brittany Michelle Chapman retained Strategic Legal
                                                        Practices APC (the Firm) to represent her in this consumer warranty
                                  18                    action. What followed was not merely inadequate representation but
                                                        an abdication of counsel’s core professional responsibility of
                                  19                    providing competent, diligent, and accountable representation. The
                                  20
                                       1
                                  21       As this Court noted in its April 28, 2026 Order:

                                  22             In Lopez, the court found that Ms. Tirmizi had violated Rule 11(b) by engaging in
                                                 “uncivil name calling and a material misrepresentation of procedural facts.”
                                  23             Lopez, 2026 WL 782497 at *2. The court emphasized that “[t]he fact that these
                                                 statements were mistakenly included because they were taken from a template
                                  24
                                                 only serves to show the degree of carelessness involved, which is inconsistent
                                  25             with an objective standard of reasonableness for an officer of the court.” Id.
                                                 Tionna Carvalho, Elizabeth LaRocque, and Rabiya Tirmizi were counsel of
                                  26             record in Lopez. The court held Ms. Tirmizi and SLP jointly responsible for
                                                 paying the sanction of $500. As discussed further in this Order, Ms. Tirmizi has
                                  27             since filed a notice of disassociation from SLP.
                                  28
                                       ECF No. 66 at 2.
                                                                                          2
                                            Case 5:24-cv-06274-NW        Document 119        Filed 07/17/26      Page 3 of 5



                                                      record reveals a volume-driven business approach to litigation—
                                   1                  marked by perfunctory line-level attention, lack of meaningful
                                                      supervision, and execution falling well below professional standards.
                                   2                  Most strikingly, counsel approved and filed critical trial documents
                                                      that effectively doomed their client’s case by requiring Plaintiff to
                                   3                  prove she purchased a “new” vehicle, despite the undisputed fact that
                                                      it was preowned. These deficiencies were further compounded by
                                   4                  counsel’s failure to conduct a reasonable factual and legal
                                                      investigation, to comply with basic pretrial obligations and court
                                   5                  orders, and to provide timely and adequate responses when called to
                                                      account. Taken together, the record reflects not isolated error, but a
                                   6                  systemic breakdown in professional responsibility warranting
                                                      sanctions.
                                   7

                                   8   Id.

                                   9           As the enormous scope of SLP’s misconduct became clear, the Court was mindful of its

                                  10   larger ethical duties. These include:

                                  11              •   Judicial Canon 1, “A judge should maintain and enforce high standards of

                                  12                  conduct;”
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13              •   The commentary to Canon 3A(5), “A judge should monitor and supervise cases to

                                  14                  reduce or eliminate dilatory practices, avoidable delays, and unnecessary costs;”

                                  15                  and

                                  16              •   The commentary to Canon 3B(6), “Public confidence in the integrity and

                                  17                  impartiality of the judiciary is promoted when judges take appropriate action based

                                  18                  on reliable information of likely misconduct. . . . Appropriate action may include

                                  19                  direct communication with the . . . lawyer, other direct action if available,

                                  20                  [including] reporting the conduct to the appropriate authorities.” 2

                                  21   See Canons 1, 3A(5), 3B(6), Code of Conduct for United States Judges [available at

                                  22   https://www.uscourts.gov/administration-policies/judiciary-policies/ethics-policies/code-conduct-

                                  23   united-states-judges].

                                  24           The Court sought to gather sufficient information to determine what constitutes an

                                  25   “appropriate action” given the unusual facts. The focus of the Court’s latter inquires into SLP has

                                  26   been on Mr. Shahian, not only because he is the firm’s founder and managing partner, but also

                                  27
                                       2
                                  28     Reporting conduct to the appropriate authorities may include making a confidential referral to a
                                       relevant assistance program.
                                                                                        3
                                         Case 5:24-cv-06274-NW            Document 119         Filed 07/17/26     Page 4 of 5




                                   1   because the Court understood that as of May 1, 2026, when Ms. Carvalho was leaving the firm,

                                   2   Mr. Shahian would be sole remaining partner at SLP.

                                   3          Despite numerous Orders issued during hearings, and in writing, Mr. Shahian did not

                                   4   comply with the Court’s Orders to Show Cause. Despite several extensions of time, he repeatedly

                                   5   failed to provide comprehensive information regarding sanctions against SLP and its attorneys

                                   6   over the last five years, asserting that he could not provide it and that the information was not

                                   7   relevant to any potential sanction in this action. It is not clear to the Court whether Mr. Shahian

                                   8   failed to provide this data because he and SLP have elected not to maintain any records about

                                   9   when SLP or its attorneys are sanctioned (including the amounts of those sanctions, if and when

                                  10   they are paid, and if and when mandatory reporting to the California State Bare was completed), or

                                  11   because the number of sanctions is so voluminous or has resulted in non-compliance with

                                  12   mandatory reporting to the State Bar, that Mr. Shahian decided it was better to violate a Court
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Order than to disclose this information to the Court. Either option reflects professional

                                  14   misconduct.

                                  15          Based only on the incomplete accounting that Mr. Shahian did disclose to the Court, SLP

                                  16   was sanctioned $23,000 from October 2025 to May 2026. This is separate from the tens of

                                  17   thousands of dollars in sanctions various courts imposed on SLP lawyers personally. Yet, this

                                  18   amount was not sufficient to deter SLP’s misconduct, see Timmerman v. FCA US, LLC, No. 25-

                                  19   CV-00400-TLT, 2026 WL 1947623, at *1 (N.D. Cal. July 6, 2026), nor was it sufficient to stop

                                  20   SLP from taking on new clients while the firm addressed its inability to professionally manage the

                                  21   cases it already had. ECF No. 113 at 3.

                                  22          As a result, and as ordered during the July 14, 2026 hearing, the Court ORDERS the

                                  23   following:

                                  24          •     The Court imposes a sanction of $25,000 against SLP, to be paid to the Clerk of the

                                  25                Court by August 13, 2026.

                                  26          •     By August 13, 2026, Mr. Shahian must provide a copy of this Order to the California

                                  27                State Bar Office of Attorney Discipline, and must also specifically report to their office

                                  28                this sanction, and all other monetary sanctions (of any amount, regardless of whether
                                                                                          4
                                         Case 5:24-cv-06274-NW          Document 119          Filed 07/17/26     Page 5 of 5




                                   1              any individual monetary sanction was below the $1,000 mandatory reportable

                                   2              threshold), that any court, state or federal, has imposed on SLP or any attorneys who

                                   3              have appeared on behalf of SLP from October 1, 2024, through the date of this Order.

                                   4          •   By July 28, 2026, Plaintiff’s counsel shall file a signed declaration from Plaintiff

                                   5              Santiago Talavera Castro indicating that he understands and accepts the Offer of

                                   6              Judgment. The Court will address the proposed judgment, ECF No. 116, after

                                   7              receiving Plaintiff’s declaration. All upcoming pretrial dates and deadlines are

                                   8              vacated.

                                   9          •   The Court discharges the Order to Show Cause.

                                  10          •   Plaintiff’s administrative motion to file under seal, ECF No. 110, is denied for lack of

                                  11              compelling reasons shown.

                                  12          IT IS SO ORDERED.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Dated: July 17, 2026

                                  14
                                                                                                    Noël Wise
